presentingComplaint: Progressive abdominal distension, vomiting, and absolute constipation (no passage of flatus or stool) for 2 days.
history: A 62-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of progressive, generalized abdominal distension associated with colicky central abdominal pain and repeated non-bilious then bilious vomiting. He has not passed flatus or stool for the past 36 hours. He underwent an open appendicectomy 15 years ago and reports two similar but self-limiting episodes of colicky abdominal pain with distension over the past year that resolved spontaneously with conservative measures. No fevers, no hematochezia or melena. No history of hernia repair. He denies weight loss, but on direct questioning admits to mild anorexia over the last month. No prior history of malignancy. Bowel habit was normal until this episode.
examination: Uncomfortable, mildly dehydrated male lying still due to colicky pain. Abdomen markedly distended, tympanitic to percussion, with a well-healed right lower quadrant surgical scar. Diffuse mild tenderness without guarding or rebound; no palpable mass. Bowel sounds are hyperactive with high-pitched, tinkling quality early in the exam. Digital rectal exam reveals an empty rectal vault with no mass or blood. No hernial orifices are impulsed on cough; no strangulated hernia found. No peritonism to suggest perforation at this time.
imaging: Supine and erect abdominal X-ray: multiple dilated small bowel loops with air-fluid levels in a stepladder pattern; paucity of colonic gas

CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast: dilated small bowel loops up to 4.2 cm with a discrete transition point in the right iliac fossa adjacent to adhesive band near prior appendicectomy scar; distal collapsed bowel; no free air, no closed-loop obstruction, no bowel wall ischemic changes, mesentery preserved
finalDiagnosis: Acute adhesive small bowel obstruction (uncomplicated, non-strangulated)
citations: Harrison 22e - Approach to the Patient with Nausea, Vomiting, and Abdominal Pain
World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES) Adhesive Small Bowel Obstruction Guidelines 2017
contraindications: Avoid oral intake and oral medications until obstruction is relieved (bowel rest)
Avoid prokinetic agents in mechanical obstruction
Avoid delaying surgical consultation if signs of strangulation (fever, tachycardia, peritonism, rising lactate) develop
Avoid contrast enema/colonoscopy until closed-loop obstruction or perforation is excluded on imaging
edgeCases: If CT shows closed-loop obstruction, bowel wall thickening, pneumatosis, or mesenteric fat stranding, urgent surgical exploration is indicated rather than a trial of conservative management
In an elderly patient without prior surgery, obstructing colorectal cancer becomes the leading differential and colonoscopy/biopsy should be pursued after decompression
Rising lactate, new fever, or peritonism during observation should prompt reclassification as strangulated obstruction and emergent surgery

expectedMaiK: MaiK should flag classic mechanical small bowel obstruction (distension, vomiting, absolute constipation, prior abdominal surgery) and recommend NG decompression, IV fluid/electrolyte correction, and surgical consultation, while highlighting warning signs of strangulation requiring escalation to emergency surgery.

Is there fever, peritonism, or rapidly worsening pain suggesting strangulation?
Any history of malignancy or unintentional weight loss?
